about.p: This course goes with *English Pronunciation in Use Elementary*. It follows the book's fifty units: the vowel and consonant sounds first, then groups of consonants, syllables and word stress, and finally how English sounds in phrases, sentences and conversation.

Every word has a sound button. Listen, copy it aloud, and tap *Say it* to see what your phone heard. The phonemic symbols, such as /iː/ or /θ/, show exactly which sound to make – Unit 1 and Reference 1 explain them.

Little and often works best: ten minutes a day does more for your pronunciation than an hour once a week. Listen to each word several times before you say it, and record yourself when you can – you will hear things you cannot notice while you speak.
The sound units can be done in any order, so start with the sounds you find hardest. Reference 5 lists the ones that Korean speakers usually need most.

about.tip: Listening questions use your device's own British voice. If you hear an American voice, or nothing at all, open the Me tab: it shows which voice your device is using and how to add a British one.

L.p: English has 26 letters but about 44 sounds. So one letter can stand for several sounds, and one sound can be written in several ways. The letter *a*, for example, sounds different in *cat*, *car*, *came* and *call*.
That is why dictionaries show pronunciation with phonemic symbols between slashes, like /kæt/. Each symbol always stands for one sound, however the word is spelt.
Some letters are written but not said: the *k* in *knee*, the *w* in *write*, the *b* in *comb*, the *s* in *island* and the *l* in *half*.
Many pairs of letters make a single sound: *sh* in *ship*, *ph* in *phone*, *ng* in *sing*, *ck* in *back*. Double letters, like the *nn* in *dinner*, are one sound too.
A few letters stand for two sounds together. *x* is usually /ks/, as in *box* and *taxi*, and *u* is often /juː/, as in *music* and *cute*.

Most consonant symbols look like ordinary letters: /p/, /b/, /t/, /d/, /m/, /s/. The vowel symbols are different, and you will learn them one or two at a time in Units 2–10. The mark /ː/ means a long sound, and /ˈ/ comes just before the stressed syllable: /ˈdɪnə/ is *dinner*.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Hangul is written almost exactly as it sounds, so it feels natural to read English the same way. English does not work like that. Check every new word with the sound button or its symbols before you trust the spelling.

L.x: The *l* in *walk* is silent, so the word is */wɔːk/* (not */wɔːlk/*).
The *w* in *answer* is silent, so the word is */ˈɑːnsə/* (not */ˈɑːnswə/*).

L.p: This unit compares two vowels that many languages – Korean included – treat as one sound. /iː/ is long and tense; /ɪ/ is short and relaxed. Changing one for the other can change the word.
Spread your lips as if you are smiling, and push your tongue high and forward. Hold the sound: the mark /ː/ means it is long.
Common spellings: *ee* (*need*), *ea* (*clean*), *e* (*she*), *ie* (*believe*) and *ei* (*receive*).

L.say: We meet at the beach each week.

L.p: Relax your lips and tongue. Your mouth is a little more open than for /iː/, and the sound is short.
/ɪ/ is nearly always spelt *i* (*sit*, *with*), but notice *busy*, *women*, *pretty* and *English*.

L.say: This is a big gift for Jim.

L.p: Compare *leave* and *live*, *seat* and *sit*, *feel* and *fill*. Make /iː/ long, with smiling lips, and keep /ɪ/ short and loose.

L.say: Can I sit in this seat?
Please fill it with cheap milk.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean 이 sits between the two English sounds. For /iː/, smile and make it longer than 이. For /ɪ/, keep it short and loose – it moves a little towards 에.

L.x: At the end of *city*, *party* and *money* the sound is a short /i/, so *city* is */ˈsɪti/* (not */ˈsɪtiː/*).

W: piece|/piːs/||Would you like a [piece] of cake?|A

X.i: Which word has a different vowel sound?
Long /iː/ or short /ɪ/?

items.why: /ˈprɪti/: here the letter e sounds like /ɪ/.

units.O: Write three sentences about your street or your town. Use at least three /iː/ words and three /ɪ/ words, then read them aloud slowly.
units.sub: the long vowel in 'leave' and the short one in 'live'

L.p: Unit 2 compared a long and a short vowel at the front of the mouth. This unit does the same at the back: /uː/ is long, with tight, round lips; /ʊ/ is short and relaxed.
Round your lips into a small circle and push them forward. Pull your tongue back and hold the sound.

Common spellings: *oo* (*food*), *u* (*rule*), *ue* (*true*), *ew* (*flew*), *ou* (*soup*) and *o* (*do*). After many consonants, *u* and *ew* have a /j/ before the vowel: *huge* /hjuːdʒ/, *few* /fjuː/, *new* /njuː/.

L.say: Do you choose soup or fruit at school?

L.p: Your lips are only a little rounded and the sound is short. It is spelt *oo* (*book*, *good*), *u* (*put*, *full*), and *ou* in *could*, *would* and *should*.

L.say: Look! The cook took a good book.

L.p: Compare *pool* and *pull*, *fool* and *full*, *Luke* and *look*. Hold /uː/ with tight lips; make /ʊ/ quick and loose.

L.say: The pool is full.

L.tip: Korean speakers: 우 is close to /uː/, but hold the English sound longer and round your lips more. For /ʊ/, relax your lips; the sound moves a little towards 어. Many learners say *full* and *fool* the same way – practise the pairs below.

L.x: *good* has the short vowel, so it is */gʊd/* (not */guːd/*).
The *oo* in *blood* is /ʌ/, so the word is */blʌd/* (not */bluːd/*).

W: pull|/pʊl/||[Pull] the door to open it.|B

X.i: Which word has a different vowel sound?
Write the word in normal spelling.

units.O: Write a shopping list of six things to eat or drink. Next to each one, write /uː/, /ʊ/ or neither, then say the list aloud.
units.sub: the long vowel in 'pool' and the short one in 'pull'

L.p: /ɑː/ is a long, open sound at the back of the mouth. /ʌ/ is short and sits in the middle of the mouth. Both are very common in British English.
Open your mouth wide, as if a doctor is looking at your throat. Keep your tongue low and back, and hold the sound.
Common spellings: *ar* (*car*, *park*), *al* (*calm*, *half*), *ear* (*heart*), and *a* in many British words such as *bath*, *fast*, *ask* and *after*.
In British English the *r* in *car*, *park* and *start* is not pronounced: you only hear the long vowel.

L.say: Park the car in the dark yard.

L.p: Open your mouth a little and relax. The sound is short. It is spelt *u* (*cup*, *bus*), *o* (*son*, *love*, *money*), *ou* (*young*, *country*) and *oo* (*blood*).

L.say: My brother's young son loves buses.

L.p: Compare *heart* and *hut*, *cart* and *cut*, *calm* and *come*. /ɑː/ is long and open; /ʌ/ is short.

L.say: Come and see the calm sea.

L.!: British speakers say *bath*, *grass*, *dance*, *after* and *can't* with the long /ɑː/. Most American speakers use the /æ/ of *cat* in these words.

L.tip: Korean speakers: 아 is close to /ɑː/ – just hold it longer. A short 어 is close to /ʌ/, so *bus* and *cup* are usually easy. The hard part is keeping the two apart: *heart* must be long, *hut* must be short.

W: cup|/kʌp/||Would you like a [cup] of tea?|B

items.why: last has /ɑː/ in British English. The others have /ʌ/.
calm has /ɑː/ and a silent l. The others have /ʌ/.

X.i: Which is the British English pronunciation?

items.why: British English uses the long vowel /ɑː/ here.
The long /ɑː/, and no /r/ at the end.

units.O: Write about your family in four sentences. Then find the /ʌ/ words (like *mother* or *brother*) and the /ɑː/ words, and say them aloud.

L.p: /ɒ/ is short and open, with slightly rounded lips. /ɔː/ is long, with lips that are rounder and further forward. Both are back vowels: your tongue is pulled back for each of them.
Open your mouth and round your lips a little. Keep the sound short.
It is usually spelt *o* (*hot*, *stop*), and *a* after *w* or *qu*: *want*, *what*, *watch*, *quality*.

L.say: Stop at the shop on the top floor.

L.p: Round your lips more and push them forward. Hold the sound, and don't let it slide.
There are many spellings: *or* (*short*), *ore* (*more*), *our* (*four*), *aw* (*saw*), *au* (*August*), *al* (*walk*), *ar* after *w* (*warm*) and *ough* (*bought*).

L.say: I saw four tall horses walk past the door.

L.p: Compare *spot* and *sport*, *pot* and *port*, *shot* and *short*. /ɒ/ is quick; /ɔː/ is long and round.

L.say: What sport do you watch?

L.!: In British English, *hot*, *stop* and *box* have /ɒ/, with rounded lips. In American English these words have a sound much closer to the /ɑː/ of *car*.

L.tip: Korean speakers: you may use 오 for /ɔː/ and for the /əʊ/ of *go* (Unit 10), so *walk* and *woke* can sound the same. /ɔː/ stays still; /əʊ/ moves. Also keep *walk* and *work* apart – they are different vowels.

L.x: Don't say *walk* like *work*: *walk* is */wɔːk/* (not */wɜːk/*).

X.i: Which word has a different vowel sound?
Write the word in normal spelling.

units.O: Write four sentences about what you do every morning. Find each /ɒ/ word and each /ɔː/ word, then read the sentences aloud.

L.p: /e/ and /æ/ are both short vowels at the front of the mouth. The difference is how far your jaw drops: a little for /e/, a lot for /æ/.
Open your mouth a little and spread your lips slightly. Keep the sound short.
It is usually spelt *e* (*ten*, *send*), but also *ea* (*bread*), *ai* (*said*), *ie* (*friend*) and *a* (*any*, *many*).

L.say: Ben sent ten letters to his friend.

L.p: Drop your jaw much lower than for /e/ and spread your lips. Your tongue is low and at the front. The sound is short, but a little longer than /e/.
It is nearly always spelt *a*: *man*, *black*, *happy*.

L.say: That man has a black bag in his hand.

L.p: Compare *bed* and *bad*, *men* and *man*, *pen* and *pan*. If they sound the same when you say them, open your mouth wider for /æ/.

L.say: Is the pen in the pan?

L.tip: Korean speakers: most people today say 애 and 에 the same way, so *bed* and *bad* can sound identical. For /æ/, open your mouth as wide as for 아 but keep your lips spread – a sound between 애 and 아.

L.x: *many* has /e/, so it is */ˈmeni/* (not */ˈmæni/*).

L.p: /ɜː/ is a long vowel made in the middle of the mouth, with relaxed lips. Many learners find it hard because their language has nothing like it – but it is in some of the most common English words: *work*, *first*, *her*, *learn*.
Open your mouth a little, keep your lips flat and relaxed – not round – and let your tongue rest in the middle. Hold the sound.
Spellings: *er* (*her*, *person*), *ir* (*first*), *ur* (*turn*), *ear* (*learn*), and *or* after *w* (*work*, *word*, *world*).

L.say: The first girl learnt thirty words.

L.p: Unit 5 had this sound. It is here to compare with /ɜː/: for /ɔː/ your lips are round and pushed forward.
Compare *walk* and *work*, *born* and *burn*, *short* and *shirt*. Round lips: /ɔː/. Flat, relaxed lips: /ɜː/.

L.say: I walk to work.
He was born on the third of March.

L.!: In British English the *r* in *her*, *first* and *work* is silent: the long vowel is all you hear. Most American speakers pronounce the r.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean has no /ɜː/, so *work* often comes out as 워크, which sounds like *walk*. Keep your lips flat (no 우 shape at the start of the vowel) and hold a long, relaxed 어.

L.x: *word* is */wɜːd/* (not */wɔːd/*).

W: world|/wɜːld/||She has travelled all over the [world].|A

X.i: Which word has a different vowel sound?
Write the word in normal spelling.

units.O: Write five sentences about your work or your studies (*I work…*, *I'm learning…*, *My first…*). Read them aloud with a long, flat /ɜː/.

L.p: /ɪə/ and /eə/ are diphthongs: vowels that start in one place and move to another. Both of these finish with the weak, relaxed /ə/.
Start with /ɪ/ and slide smoothly to /ə/. It is one syllable, not two.
Common spellings: *ear* (*near*), *eer* (*beer*), *ere* (*here*) and *ea* (*idea*).

L.say: Come and sit near here, dear.

L.p: Start with /e/ and slide to /ə/. Many younger British speakers hardly move at all: they say a long /e/, like *hair* /heː/.
Common spellings: *air* (*chair*), *are* (*care*), *ere* (*where*), *ear* (*wear*) and *eir* (*their*).

L.say: Where are their chairs?

L.p: *ear* can be either sound, so learn each word: *hear* has /ɪə/, but *bear* and *wear* have /eə/.

L.say: Can you hear the bear?

L.!: In British English, there is no /r/ sound at the end of *near*, *beer*, *hair* or *where* – unless the next word begins with a vowel (see Unit 34).

L.tip: Korean speakers: say 이어 or 에어 as one quick syllable, not two, and do not add an American-style r at the end.

L.x: *wear* has /eə/, so it is */weə/* (not */wɪə/*).

W: pair|/peə/||I need a new [pair] of shoes.|B
airport|/ˈeəpɔːt/||I'll pick you up at the [airport].|B|Oo

Choose the right word.

units.O: Describe someone you know: their hair, what they usually wear and where they live. Say each /ɪə/ and /eə/ as one smooth sound.

L.p: These three diphthongs all slide towards /ɪ/. They start in different places: /eɪ/ starts at /e/, /aɪ/ starts with an open /a/, and /ɔɪ/ starts with round lips.
Start with /e/ and slide up to /ɪ/. Don't cut it short: *late* is not *let*.
Spellings: *a* + consonant + *e* (*name*), *ai* (*rain*), *ay* (*day*), *ey* (*they*), *eigh* (*eight*) and *ea* in *great*, *break* and *steak*.

L.say: They waited eight days for the train.

L.p: Open your mouth wide, then slide up to /ɪ/.
Spellings: *i* + consonant + *e* (*time*), *y* (*my*), *igh* (*night*), *ie* (*tie*) and *uy* (*buy*).

L.say: I like riding my bike at night.

L.p: Start with round lips, as for /ɔː/, and slide to /ɪ/.
It is spelt *oi* (*coin*) or *oy* (*boy*).

L.say: The boy enjoyed the noise.

L.p: Compare *buy* and *boy*, *tie* and *toy*, *lake* and *like*, *wait* and *wet*.

L.say: Did you buy a toy for the boy?

L.tip: Korean speakers: 에이, 아이 and 오이 are two syllables in Korean, but each English diphthong is one syllable that glides. Say *day* as one beat, not 데-이.

L.x: *said* does not have the sound of *say*: it is */sed/* (not */seɪd/*).

W: buy|/baɪ/||I want to [buy] a new phone.|B
coin|/kɔɪn/||I found a [coin] on the floor.|C

X.i: Which word has a different vowel sound?

items.why: speak has /iː/. The others have /eɪ/ – a surprising spelling.

X.i: Which letter's name has the same vowel sound?

items.why: A, H, J and K all have /eɪ/.
B, C, D, E, G, P, T and V all have /iː/.

units.O: Write about your perfect day off: what time you get up, what you like doing and what you enjoy most. Say each /eɪ/, /aɪ/ and /ɔɪ/ as one smooth, sliding sound.

L.p: /əʊ/ and /aʊ/ both slide towards /ʊ/, with the lips rounding at the end. /əʊ/ starts in the middle of the mouth; /aʊ/ starts wide open.
Start with a relaxed /ə/ and round your lips as you slide to /ʊ/.
Spellings: *o* (*go*), *o* + consonant + *e* (*home*), *oa* (*road*), *ow* (*know*) and *ou* (*though*).

L.say: Don't go home alone on the cold road.

L.p: Open your mouth wide, then close it and round your lips as you slide to /ʊ/.
It is spelt *ow* (*now*, *town*) or *ou* (*house*, *out*).

L.say: How about a house in town?

L.p: The spelling *ow* can be either sound: *know* has /əʊ/, but *now* has /aʊ/. Learn each word with its sound.

L.say: I know, but not now.

L.!: The British /əʊ/ starts from a central /ə/. In American English the same words (*go*, *home*, *phone*) start from a sound closer to /o/.

L.tip: Korean speakers: 오 does not move, but /əʊ/ does. Start from a relaxed 어 and glide to 우, quickly: *go* is close to a fast 거우, not 고. /aʊ/ is like 아우 said as one syllable.

L.x: *go* slides to /ʊ/, so it is */gəʊ/* (not */gɔː/*).

X.i: Which word has a different vowel sound?
Write the word in normal spelling.

items.why: Both words sound exactly the same.

units.O: Write five sentences about your home town: where it is, what you can do there and how people get around. Read them aloud, sliding each /əʊ/ and /aʊ/.

L.p: /p/ and /b/ are both made with the lips. You close them, build up air, and open them suddenly. The difference is your voice: /p/ is voiceless, /b/ is voiced.
At the start of a word there is a strong puff of air after /p/. Hold your hand close to your lips: you can feel the air on *pie*, but hardly any on *buy*.
It is spelt *p* or *pp* (*pepper*). A few words have a silent *p*: *receipt*, *cupboard*.

L.say: Please pack the paper cups.

L.p: Close your lips and use your voice. Put your hand on your throat: you can feel it buzz.
It is spelt *b* or *bb* (*rubbish*). The *b* is silent after *m* (*comb*, *thumb*, *climb*) and in *doubt* and *debt*.

L.say: Bob bought a big blue bag.

L.p: At the end of a word, a vowel before /b/ is a little longer than a vowel before /p/: compare *cap* and *cab*, *rope* and *robe*.

L.say: Pay the bill, please.

L.tip: Korean speakers: ㅍ makes a good English /p/ at the start of a word. For /b/, think of the soft ㅂ in the middle of 아버지 – it is voiced, just like English /b/. At the end of a word Korean ㅂ is not released, so *cap* and *cab* both become 캡: make the vowel in *cab* longer and let your lips open gently.

L.x: *climb* has a silent *b*, so it is */klaɪm/* (not */klaɪmb/*).

W: bear|/beə/||A [bear] came out of the trees.|B

X.i: Which word has a silent letter?

units.O: Make a list of the things you would pack for a weekend away. Say every /p/ with a puff of air and every /b/ with your voice on.

L.p: /t/ and /d/ are made with the tip of your tongue on the hard ridge just behind your top teeth. /t/ is voiceless; /d/ is voiced.
Press your tongue tip on the ridge, then let the air go. At the start of a word there is a puff of air, as with /p/.
It is spelt *t* or *tt* (*better*), and *-ed* is /t/ after some sounds (*walked* – see Unit 43). The *t* is silent in *listen*, *castle* and *Christmas*.

L.say: Tom wants two cups of tea at ten.

L.p: Put your tongue in the same place and use your voice.
It is spelt *d* or *dd* (*ladder*), and *-ed* is often /d/ (*played*). The first *d* in *Wednesday* is silent.

L.say: Dan's dad drove down the road.

L.p: Compare *try* and *dry*, *write* and *ride*, *bet* and *bed*. When a word ends in /d/, the vowel before it is held a little longer.

L.say: Write it down.

L.!: In careful British English the *t* in *water*, *better* and *city* is a clear /t/. In American English it sounds more like a quick /d/. Many British people drop it in casual speech (*wa'er*), but the clear /t/ is the safest model.

L.tip: Korean speakers: ㅌ is a good /t/, and the soft ㄷ in the middle of 바다 is close to /d/. Don't add 으 after a final /t/ or /d/: *bed* is one syllable, not 베드.

L.x: *Wednesday* has a silent first *d*, so it is */ˈwenzdeɪ/* (not */ˈwednesdeɪ/*).

W: die|/daɪ/||My plants [die] if I forget to water them.|B

X.i: Which word has a silent t or d?

items.why: Wednesday /ˈwenzdeɪ/: the first d is silent.
castle /ˈkɑːsl/: the t is silent. In the others, tt is /t/.

units.O: Write about what you did yesterday, from morning to night. Say every /t/ and /d/ clearly, especially at the ends of words.

L.p: /k/ and /g/ are made at the back of the mouth: the back of your tongue presses against the soft part of the roof of your mouth. /k/ is voiceless; /g/ is voiced.
Press the back of your tongue up and let the air go with a puff.
Spellings: *c* (*cold*), *k* (*kind*), *ck* (*duck*), *ch* (*Christmas*, *stomach*) and *qu*, which is /kw/ (*quick*). The *k* in *knee* and *know* is silent.

L.say: Can Kate cook a quick cake?

L.p: Use the same place and add your voice.
Spellings: *g* (*big*), *gg* (*bigger*), *gu* (*guess*, *guitar*). Before *e*, *i* and *y*, *g* is sometimes /dʒ/ instead (*giant*, *gym* – see Unit 18).

L.say: The girl gave the goat a green bag.

L.p: Compare *coat* and *goat*, *class* and *glass*, *back* and *bag*. As with /p/–/b/ and /t/–/d/, the vowel is longer before /g/.

L.say: Come and play a game.

L.tip: Korean speakers: ㅋ is a good /k/, and the ㄱ in the middle of 아기 is close to /g/. At the end of a word, Korean ㄱ is not released, so *back* and *bag* can both sound like 백: lengthen the vowel in *bag* and let the /g/ go gently.

L.x: *stomach* ends in /k/, so it is */ˈstʌmək/* (not */ˈstʌmətʃ/*).

W: class|/klɑːs/||There are twenty people in my [class].|A
dug|/dʌg/||We [dug] a hole in the garden.|B

units.O: Write down five things you can see in your kitchen. Which have /k/, and which have /g/? Say them aloud.

L.p: /f/ and /v/ are made with your top teeth gently touching your lower lip. /f/ is voiceless – just air; /v/ is voiced – it buzzes.
Rest your top teeth on your lower lip and blow.
Spellings: *f* and *ff* (*off*), *ph* (*photo*) and *gh* in a few words (*laugh*, *enough*).

L.say: Five friends found a fast ferry.

L.p: Keep your teeth on your lip and add your voice. It should feel a little ticklish.
It is spelt *v*, and the *f* in *of* is /v/ too.

L.say: Vicky visited seven villages.

L.p: Compare *fan* and *van*, *few* and *view*, *safe* and *save*.

L.say: We saved a few pounds on the view.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean has no /f/ or /v/, so they are often replaced with ㅍ and ㅂ: *coffee* becomes 커피 and *video* becomes 비디오. That turns *fork* into *pork* and *very* into *berry*! The cure is simple: your top teeth must touch your lower lip for every /f/ and /v/. Check in a mirror.

L.p: For /l/, the tip of your tongue presses on the ridge behind your top teeth, and the air goes out round the sides of your tongue. English has two kinds of /l/, depending on where it comes in the word.

L.h: A /l/ before a vowel, as in "look"

L.p: Before a vowel the /l/ is "clear": the front of your tongue is high, and the sound is bright, a little like /iː/.

L.say: Lucy likes lemon and lime.

L.h: B /l/ at the end, as in "ball"

L.p: At the end of a word, or before a consonant, the /l/ is "dark": the back of your tongue rises too, so it sounds deeper, a little like /ʊ/. Your tongue tip still touches the ridge.

L.p: The British /r/ is soft. Your tongue does not touch the roof of your mouth and it does not roll or tap. And in standard British English, you only say /r/ when a vowel comes after it.

L.h: A /r/ before a vowel, as in "run"

L.p: Curl the tip of your tongue up and back a little, towards the ridge, but don't touch it. Round your lips slightly. Now let your voice flow into the vowel.

L.say: Rob ran round the red rocks.

L.h: B r after a vowel: silent, as in "car"

L.p: When *r* comes after a vowel and there is no vowel after it, you don't say it in British English: *car* /kɑː/, *door* /dɔː/, *never* /ˈnevə/. The *r* usually just tells you the vowel is long.

L.say: Our teacher's car is parked near the door.

L.p: If the next word starts with a vowel, the silent *r* is pronounced to link the words: *far away* /fɑːr əˈweɪ/, *four o'clock* /fɔːr əˈklɒk/, *her arm*.

L.say: Is it far away? No, it's near enough.

L.!: This is one of the clearest differences between British and American English. Most Americans say /r/ in *car*, *park* and *water*; British speakers don't.

L.tip: Korean speakers: ㄹ between vowels is a quick tap, and English listeners hear it as /d/ or /l/. For English /r/, keep your tongue away from the roof of your mouth. A good way in: say 우, then slowly move into *red* without touching anything.

L.p: These groups usually begin with *ex-*: the *x* is two sounds, /k/ + /s/, and then come one or two more.
Practise slowly first, then faster. If a group is hard, build the word up from the end: *-dred*, *-undred*, *hundred*.

L.say: We must go – the last train leaves in ten minutes.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean also joins words in speech, so you already know the idea. The difference is that English never adds a vowel between words. Keep *big dog* to two syllables.

L.p: A syllable is one beat of a word. Each syllable has one vowel sound at its centre, often with consonants before or after it. Clap as you say a word: one clap, one syllable.
Count vowel sounds, not vowel letters. *made* has two vowel letters but only one vowel sound, /eɪ/, so it has one syllable.
Some English words have lots of letters but only one syllable: *jumped*, *months*, *clothes*.

L.h: Words that are shorter than they look

L.p: Some common words lose a vowel in normal speech. *Wednesday* /ˈwenzdeɪ/ and *business* /ˈbɪznəs/ have two syllables; *vegetable* /ˈvedʒtəbl/ and *comfortable* /ˈkʌmftəbl/ have three.

L.say: I bought some vegetables on Wednesday.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean syllables end with a vowel or one consonant, so English loanwords gain extra syllables – 스트레스 has four, but *stress* has one. When you clap an English word, check that you haven't added 으 or 이.

L.p: In English, syllables are not all equal. A stressed syllable has a strong vowel; many unstressed syllables have a weak vowel. The most common weak vowel is /ə/, called schwa. It is the most frequent vowel sound in English.

/ə/ is short, quiet and relaxed: open your mouth a little, relax your lips and tongue, and make a very short sound. It can be spelt with any vowel letter: *a*bout, op*e*n, p*o*lice, s*u*pport, doct*or*, teach*er*, fam*ou*s.

L.h: A /ə/ in the first syllable, as in "away"
B /ə/ in the last syllable, as in "sofa"
C /ə/ in the middle, as in "Saturday"

L.p: The same letters can be strong in one word and weak in another. Listen to the *o* in *photo* /ˈfəʊtəʊ/, *photograph* /ˈfəʊtəgrɑːf/ and *photographer* /fəˈtɒgrəfə/ – the stress moves, and the weak vowels move with it.

L.say: A banana for the doctor's daughter.

L.p: You will also hear a weak /ɪ/ in some unstressed syllables, such as *minute* /ˈmɪnɪt/ and *village* /ˈvɪlɪdʒ/, and a short /i/ at the end of *happy* and *city*.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean has no schwa, and it gives every vowel its full value, so *banana* becomes 바나나 with three equal syllables. In English only the middle syllable is strong: bə-NAA-nə. Make the weak vowels very short – like a quick, lazy 어.

L.x: *police* starts with a weak vowel, so it is */pəˈliːs/* (not */pɒˈliːs/*).

L.p: In a word with two or more syllables, one syllable is stressed: it is longer, louder and a little higher than the others. Dictionaries put the mark /ˈ/ before it: /ˈpensl/, /bɪˈgɪn/. In this course we also show the pattern with circles: *Oo* means the first syllable is stressed, *oO* means the second.

L.h: A stress on the first syllable: Oo

L.p: Most two-syllable nouns and adjectives are like this: *pencil*, *yellow*, *student*.

L.say: The student's pencil is yellow.

L.h: B stress on the second syllable: oO

L.p: Many two-syllable verbs are like this, especially when the first syllable is a short beginning such as *be-*, *for-*, *re-* or *in-*: *begin*, *forget*, *relax*, *invite*. There are exceptions in both groups, so learn the stress with every new word.

L.say: Don't forget to relax in July.

L.p: A few words are nouns with Oo and verbs with oO: a *PREsent* but to *preSENT*, a *REcord* but to *reCORD*, an *INcrease* but to *inCREASE*.

L.say: They want to record a new world record.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean gives each syllable about the same weight, but English needs one strong syllable and one weak one. Make the stressed syllable clearly longer and louder: *HO-tel* sounds wrong to English ears; *ho-TEL* sounds right.

L.x: *hotel* is stressed on the second syllable, so it is */həʊˈtel/* (not */ˈhəʊtel/*).

L.p: Longer words also have one main stress. With three syllables there are three possible patterns: *Ooo*, *oOo* and *ooO*. Words of three syllables or more often have a lighter, second stress as well, but the main one is what matters most.
These words have a lighter beat at the start and their main stress at the end.

Some endings tell you where the stress goes. With *-tion*, *-sion*, *-ic* and *-ity*, stress the syllable just before the ending: *inforMAtion*, *deCIsion*, *fanTAStic*, *uniVERsity*. Words ending in *-ese*, *-eer* and *-ee* are stressed on the ending itself: *ChiNESE*, *volunTEER*, *refuGEE*.

L.say: The engineer from Japan says it's fantastic.

L.tip: Korean speakers: in Korean loanwords every syllable has the same weight – 컴퓨터. In *computer* only the middle syllable is strong: com-PU-ter. Make the stressed syllable long, loud and high, and squash the others.

L.x: *photographer* moves the stress, so it is */fəˈtɒgrəfə/* (not */ˈfəʊtəgrɑːfə/*).

L.p: A compound is two words used together as one: *bus stop*, *birthday*, *post office*. Some are written as one word, some as two, and some with a hyphen – the spelling doesn't tell you the stress.

L.h: A first part stressed, as in "BUS stop"

L.p: Most compound nouns are stressed on the first part: *BEDroom*, *TOOTHbrush*, *CAR park*, *SWIMming pool*.

L.say: Meet me in the car park by the post office.

L.h: B second part stressed, as in "well-KNOWN"

L.p: Compound adjectives, many place words and *-teen* numbers usually have the main stress on the second part: *second-HAND*, *downSTAIRS*, *fifTEEN*.

L.say: My brand-new bike is downstairs.

L.p: Stress helps you hear numbers: *thirTEEN* has the stress at the end, but *THIRty* has it at the start. When someone says a number, listen for where the strong syllable is.

L.say: Thirteen or thirty? Fifteen or fifty?

L.!: British street names follow a pattern: with *Street*, the first word is stressed – *OXford Street*. With *Road*, *Square* or *Park*, the last word is stressed – *Abbey ROAD*, *Hyde PARK*.

L.tip: Korean speakers: say the stressed part of a compound longer and higher, and let the other part fall away. *BEDroom* is one word with one strong beat, not two equal words.

L.x: *bedroom* is stressed on the first part, so it is *BEDroom* (not *bedROOM*).

L.p: Nobody says a long sentence in one breath. We divide speech into chunks – groups of words that belong together – with a short pause between them. Each chunk has one word that stands out a little, usually near the end of the chunk.
Pause at commas and full stops, after a long subject, and before words like *and*, *but* and *because*. Keep each chunk together: *a cup of tea* is one chunk, so never pause inside it.
*When I got home | I made a cup of tea | and sat down by the window.*

L.say: When I got home, I made a cup of tea and sat down by the window.

L.p: *My friend from university | is coming to stay | next weekend.*

L.say: My friend from university is coming to stay next weekend.

L.p: Before you read a text aloud, look through it and mark the chunks. Then read each chunk smoothly, stress its most important word, and pause at the end. Slow down – a clear speaker with pauses is easier to follow than a fast one without them.

L.say: The library is closed on Sundays, but you can return books through the box by the door.

L.tip: Korean speakers: in Korean you often pause after a particle such as 은/는 or 을/를. In English, keep a whole phrase together – *the girl in the red coat* is one chunk – and pause where the meaning breaks, not after every word.

L.p: In natural speech, words are joined together. When one word ends with a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, the consonant moves across to start the next word. *Turn it off* sounds like *tur-ni-toff*.

This linking is why English can sound like one long word to learners. Once you know about it, it is much easier to hear where the words are – and your own English sounds smoother. The mark ‿ shows the link.

L.say: Pick it up and put it on the table.
Come in and sit down – I'll be back in half an hour.

L.p: Linking can make two phrases sound alike: *an ice man* and *a nice man*, *an aim* and *a name*. In real speech the meaning usually tells you which one it is.

L.say: An ice cream for a nice man.

L.!: The silent British *r* at the end of a word comes back before a vowel, as in *far away* and *four o'clock* (see Unit 22). This linking /r/ is a very British sound.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean does the same thing – 먹어 is said 머거 – so the idea is not new. Apply it to English: *get up* is said *ge-tup*, with no stop and no 으 between the words.

L.p: When a word ends with a vowel and the next word also starts with a vowel, English slips in a tiny /j/ or /w/ to join them smoothly. You don't write it, but you can hear it.

L.h: A a little /j/ joins the words, as in "say it"

L.p: After words ending in /iː/, /ɪ/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/ or /ɔɪ/ – sounds made with the tongue high at the front – a light /j/ joins the next vowel: *see it* /siː‿jɪt/, *my arm* /maɪ‿jɑːm/.

L.say: I agree, and they agree too.

L.h: B a little /w/ joins the words, as in "go away"

L.p: After words ending in /uː/, /əʊ/ or /aʊ/ – sounds made with round lips – a light /w/ joins the next vowel: *go out* /gəʊ‿waʊt/, *two eggs* /tuː‿wegz/.

L.say: Who is it? Go and open the door.

L.p: Without the link, you have to stop between the two vowels, and your English sounds jumpy. With it, the words flow. You don't need to make the /j/ or /w/ strong – just move smoothly from one vowel to the next.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean often joins two vowels in the same way (아이 can sound like 아-이 with a glide). Let your mouth keep moving between the words instead of stopping.

L.p: English has a strong rhythm, like a drum beat. The beats fall on stressed syllables, and the unstressed syllables between them are squeezed in quickly. So a long sentence with the same number of beats takes almost the same time as a short one.

Words that carry the meaning are usually stressed: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, negatives such as *not* and *never*, and question words. Grammar words are usually unstressed: *a*, *the*, *to*, *of*, *and*, pronouns and helping verbs such as *can* and *was*.

L.say: Buy new shoes. Buy some new shoes. I'm going to buy some new shoes.

L.p: *WHERE did you PUT my KEYS?* | *I've LEFT them on the TAble in the KITchen.*

L.say: Where did you put my keys? I've left them on the table in the kitchen.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean gives each syllable about the same length, so English said the Korean way can sound like a typewriter. Make the stressed syllables longer and stronger, and let the small words go fast and soft. Don't worry about saying every word clearly – the beats carry the meaning.

L.p: Many small words have two pronunciations: a strong form, used when the word is stressed, and a weak form, used when it isn't. Weak forms are normal in good British English – they are not lazy or careless.
Object pronouns are usually weak. *him* and *her* often lose their /h/, so *tell him* sounds like *tel-lim*, and *ask her* like *ask-a*.
A pronoun is strong when it is stressed for contrast or emphasis: *I didn't ask HIM – I asked HER.* It is also strong when it is said on its own: *Who, me?*

L.say: Tell him I'll call him later.
I gave it to them, not to you.

L.tip: Korean speakers: you may say every word fully, so *tell him* sounds like 텔 힘. Native speakers will understand you, but you will find their weak forms hard to hear. Practise the weak forms aloud, and you will start to hear them too.

L.p: More small words with weak forms: possessives such as *your*, conjunctions such as *and* and *but*, and prepositions such as *to*, *for*, *from*, *of* and *at*. In their weak forms, the vowel becomes /ə/ – or disappears.
*and* is often just /ən/ or even /n/: *fish and chips* /ˌfɪʃ ən ˈtʃɪps/.
Before a consonant, *of* can be just /ə/: *a cup of tea* /ə ˈkʌp ə ˈtiː/.

At the end of a sentence, a preposition is strong: *Where are you from?* /frɒm/, *Who's it for?* /fɔː/, *What are you looking at?* /æt/. It is also strong when you stress it: *Is this present from you or for you?*

L.say: I'm from Busan. Where are you from?
It's a present for you. Who's it for?

L.tip: Korean speakers: if you say *to* as 투 and *for* as 포 every time, your sentences will sound slow and heavy. In the middle of a sentence, make them short and weak: /tə/, /fə/.

L.p: Helping verbs – *can*, *was*, *were*, *does*, *do*, *have*, *are* – are usually weak in the middle of a sentence: *can* /kən/, *was* /wəz/, *were* /wə/, *does* /dəz/. They are strong at the end of a sentence, in short answers, and when you stress them.

L.p: Negatives are never weak: *wasn't*, *doesn't* and *weren't* are always stressed.

L.p: In speech, helping verbs and *not* are usually shortened and joined to the word before them: *I am* becomes *I'm*, *do not* becomes *don't*. These contractions are normal in conversation and informal writing. The full forms sound careful – or they show emphasis: *I am listening!*

*'s* can mean *is* or *has*, and *'d* can mean *would* or *had*. The rest of the sentence tells you which one it is.

L.p: The -s ending is used for plurals (*cats*), the *he/she/it* form of verbs (*works*), possessives (*Mark's*) and short forms of *is* and *has* (*it's*). It has three pronunciations, and the same rule works for all of them: it depends on the last sound before the ending.
After a voiceless sound – /p/, /t/, /k/, /f/ or /θ/ – the ending is a voiceless /s/: *cups*, *cats*, *books*, *laughs*.
After a vowel or a voiced sound – /b/, /d/, /g/, /v/, /ð/, /m/, /n/, /ŋ/ or /l/ – the ending is a voiced /z/: *days*, *dogs*, *lives*, *rooms*.
After a hissing or hushing sound – /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/ or /dʒ/ – the ending is /ɪz/, and the word gets an extra syllable: *buses*, *watches*, *oranges*.

L.say: The cats chase the dogs past the buses.

L.tip: Korean speakers: don't drop the ending – it carries grammar – and don't add 으 to it either: *cats* is one syllable, not 캣츠. Only the /ɪz/ ending adds a syllable.

L.p: Intonation is the music of speech: the way your voice goes up and down. In each chunk, your voice moves most on one stressed word – the main stress. Where you put it, and which way your voice moves, tells the listener what is new and what is important.
When you give new information, or answer a question, your voice falls on the main stressed word: *I'm from ↘Busan.* *It's on the ↘left.*

L.say: I'm from Busan. It's on the left.

L.p: When something is already known, or when you mean "…but there's more to say", your voice falls and then rises again: *↘↗Today I'm busy* (but tomorrow I'm free). *The ↘↗food was good* (but the service wasn't).

L.say: Today I'm busy, but tomorrow I'm free.

L.p: The main stress goes on the new information, so it moves during a conversation. A: *What's your ↘name?* B: *↘Sam. What's ↘yours?* *Yours* is stressed because it is the new focus.

L.say: What's your name? Sam. What's yours?

L.tip: Korean speakers: if your voice stays flat, English listeners find it hard to tell what is important, and you may sound bored when you are not. Let your voice move clearly on the main word – a big, confident fall for new information.

L.p: When you tell a story, intonation helps your listener follow it. A rise or a fall-rise at the end of a chunk says "there's more coming"; a fall says "this part is finished".
*When I got to the ↘↗station, | the train had ↘gone.* The fall-rise on *station* keeps the listener waiting; the fall on *gone* completes the idea.

L.say: When I got to the station, the train had gone.

L.p: Good storytellers guide the listener with words such as *So*, *Anyway*, *Suddenly* and *In the end*, and they pause just before the exciting part: *And then | suddenly | the lights went out.*

L.say: So I opened the door, and suddenly the lights went out.

L.p: Stress the words that move the story on – the people, places, times and actions – and say the rest more quickly.

L.say: Last Friday, at about midnight, my neighbour knocked on my door.

L.tip: Korean speakers: Korean often shows "wait, there's more" with an ending such as -는데. English does the same job with intonation: a rising or fall-rise chunk keeps the listener waiting, and a clear fall tells them the sentence is complete.

L.p: Good conversation needs good listening, and English listeners show interest with short replies: *Really?*, *Oh no!*, *That's great!* The tune matters as much as the words. A lively voice that moves a lot sounds interested; a flat voice sounds bored – or even rude.
You can also show interest with a short question made from the speaker's own words. Use a rising voice: A: *I've just got back from Japan.* B: *↗Have you?* or *↗Japan?*

L.say: I've just got back from Japan. Have you? How was it?

L.tip: Korean speakers: in Korean, listeners often show they are listening with 네 or 응. English listeners use more words, and they move their voice more. A flat "Really." can sound as if you don't believe the speaker – start high and let your voice move.

L.p: Many everyday phrases have a typical tune. Using it makes you sound friendly and polite; using the wrong one can change the meaning.
Thanks and greetings usually start high and fall: *↘Thank you.* *Good ↘morning.* A high start and a clear fall sound warm; a low, flat one sounds unfriendly.

L.say: Thank you very much. Good morning!

L.h: B saying sorry and getting attention

L.p: *Sorry* with a fall means "I apologise". *Sorry?* with a rise means "What did you say?" – and so does the slightly more formal *Pardon?* In the same way, *Excuse me?* with a rise gets someone's attention, and *Excuse me* with a fall asks someone to let you pass.

L.say: I'm sorry. Sorry? Could you say that again?

L.p: In a request, a voice that rises, or falls and then rises, sounds polite. A flat fall can sound like an order.

L.say: Could you help me? Can I have the bill, please?

L.tip: Korean speakers: politeness in Korean is shown mainly by verb endings such as -요 and -습니다. In English, polite words such as *please* and *could you* are only half of it – the other half is a friendly, moving tune.

L.p: Questions, offers, suggestions and replies also have typical tunes. Here are the most useful ones.
Questions that you answer with *yes* or *no* – including most offers – usually rise at the end: *Would you like a ↗drink?*

L.p: Suggestions often start high and fall: *Why don't we go ↘out?* *How about a ↘walk?*

L.p: Replies usually fall, and a clear fall sounds sure and friendly: *Yes, ↘please.* *No, ↘thanks.* *That sounds ↘great.*

Questions with *what*, *where*, *when*, *who* and *how* usually fall: *Where do you ↘live?* In a choice, the voice rises on the first item and falls on the last: *Tea ↗or ↘coffee?* With a question tag, a fall means you expect the listener to agree (*It's lovely, ↘isn't it?*), and a rise means you really don't know (*You're from Seoul, ↗aren't you?*).

L.say: Where do you live? Tea or coffee? It's a lovely day, isn't it?

L.p: The names of the English letters fall into seven groups by their vowel sound. Learn them in groups – it makes spelling names, emails and addresses aloud much easier.

t: B, C, D, E, G, P, T, V
F, L, M, N, S, X, Z

L.!: In British English, Z is /zed/. Americans say /ziː/.

L.h: Letters that are easy to mix up

L.p: E /iː/ and I /aɪ/; G /dʒiː/ and J /dʒeɪ/; A /eɪ/ and R /ɑː/. W /ˈdʌbljuː/ has three syllables, and H is /eɪtʃ/, although many British people say /heɪtʃ/.
For two letters the same, say *double*: *Anna* is "A, double N, A". In an email address, @ is *at* and . is *dot*: *sam.lee@mail.com* is "sam dot lee at mail dot com".

L.say: A, double N, A. Sam dot Lee at mail dot com.

L.tip: Korean speakers: say R as a long /ɑː/ with no r sound at the end (not 알), and keep E and I, and G and J, clearly apart – they are the letters that cause most spelling mistakes on the phone.

L.p: In British English, say *and* after the hundreds: 105 is *a hundred and five*, and 2,350 is *two thousand, three hundred and fifty*.

L.say: A hundred and five. Two thousand, three hundred and fifty.

L.p: 0 is *oh* in phone numbers and room numbers, *zero* for temperatures, *nil* in football scores, and *nought* or *zero* in maths (*nought point five*).
Say each digit separately, in groups of two, three or four, and use *double* for two the same: 01632 960 554 is "oh one six three two, nine six oh, double five four".
Years: 1998 is *nineteen ninety-eight*; 2008 is *two thousand and eight*; 2026 is *twenty twenty-six*. Dates: write *5 May*, but say *the fifth of May* or *May the fifth*.

L.say: The fifth of May, twenty twenty-six.

L.p: £3.50 is *three pounds fifty*; 75p is *seventy-five p* /piː/ or *seventy-five pence*; 2.5 is *two point five*; 25% is *twenty-five per cent*.

L.say: Three pounds fifty. Two point five. Twenty-five per cent.

L.p: Stress the end of *-teen* numbers (*fourTEEN*) and the start of *-ty* numbers (*FORty*). If a number really matters – a price, a time, a gate at the airport – check it: "Was that one-four or four-oh?"
Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and meanings. The situation almost always tells you which one is meant.

L.!: Because the British *r* after a vowel is silent, some pairs that sound different in American English sound the same in British English: *father* and *farther*, *sauce* and *source*, *caught* and *court*, *saw* and *sore*.
